instruction: Independently check each original natural-language question, formula solution, rubric and cited local support. Inspect the exact local declaration and its hypotheses. Treat authored support/boundary claims as claims to audit. Explain which parts the cited Lean does not prove. No earlier reviewer verdict is supplied. There is no equivalent Lean task and no anonymous Lean reconstruction to certify; do not create one. Return accept, repair-required or reject with mathematical, support and scoring evidence, explicit source-assumption differences and unresolved repair requests. Do not edit the catalog or prior reports. This is editorial review, not theorem publication or a measured benchmark run.

assumptions: On ℝᵈ with d≥1 and Lebesgue reference measure, V is a finite real-valued Borel measurable convex function. Set ρ(x)=exp(−V(x)).
mathematical_cores.boundary: No Gibbs normalization or tail-integrability theorem is supplied by the log-concavity leaf.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Identify the positive shape, logarithm, reference measure and normalizing constant; no tail-integrability proof is requested.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The existing declaration supports the positive log-concavity claim only. This full definition/normalization QA has no aligned Lean view.
mathematical_cores.question: Identify the log-concave shape and its logarithm. What additional numerical condition on Z=∫ρ(x)dx is required before ρ/Z defines a probability density? State which reference measure the word density refers to.

rubric.criterion: Identifies ρ=exp(−V)>0 and log ρ=−V.
Relates concavity of log ρ to convexity of V.
States 0<Z<∞ and p=ρ/Z rather than treating shape as already normalized.
Names Lebesgue reference measure and keeps integrability separate from shape.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original introductory exercise over the local positive log-concavity API; no textbook prose is reproduced.
steps: The shape ρ is strictly positive and Borel measurable. Its logarithm is −V, a concave function by convexity of V, so this is a positive log-concave shape.
The normalizing quantity is \[Z=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-V(x)}\,dx.\] A probability normalization requires 0<Z<∞, after which p(x)=ρ(x)/Z integrates to one against Lebesgue measure.

Log-concavity of the shape is a pointwise convex-analysis property; the finite integral is a separate analytic condition. This question asks to identify that obligation, not to prove that it holds for every convex potential.
For example V=0 has the log-concave shape ρ=1 but infinite Lebesgue integral on ℝᵈ. Thus the shape alone is not a normalized sampling target.
mathematical_cores.title: A log-concave shape is not yet a probability density

assumptions: π and ν are probability measures. K is a Markov transition kernel. C is the nonnegative random number of oracle calls in a specified run, under its actual input law.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No actual algorithm law, invariant distribution or query-cost result is constructed here.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Distinguish the objects and quantities in three common research guarantees without proving their implications.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The cited formal component concerns event discrepancy under a common Markov kernel. It is support for one guarantee type, not an aligned proof of this terminology QA or an expected-cost theorem.
mathematical_cores.question: Explain separately the meanings of TV(ν,π)≤ε, πK=π and E[C]≤B. Which objects occur in each claim, and why should a theorem statement name the run/input law when discussing expected cost? No implication among the claims needs to be proved.

rubric.criterion: Defines the event-supremum TV comparison and identifies both laws.
Explains πK=π as a one-step invariance identity.
Identifies the nonnegative cost variable and its governing run/input law.
Does not conflate output error, invariance and expected cost.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original introductory classification exercise for source-grounded sampling research claims.
steps: The first claim compares two probability laws: \[\operatorname{TV}(\nu,\pi)=\sup_{A\text{ measurable}}|\nu(A)-\pi(A)|\le\varepsilon.\] Here the convention has no extra factor of two.
The identity πK=π is invariance of the law π under one application of K. It is a statement about the kernel and its target law, not a bound on ν or a running time.
The expectation E[C]≤B concerns an algorithmic cost random variable and the probability law governing the run. Different input laws or stopping/cap rules can change that expectation.
These are different theorem outputs. A proof of one should not be relabelled as a proof of another; mixing, actual-input error and expected query cost require their own links.
mathematical_cores.title: What kind of guarantee does a sampling claim describe?

assumptions: f is differentiable on a real finite-dimensional Euclidean space and attains its global minimum f* at z. Let α>0. Use the convention 2α(f(x)−f*)≤‖∇f(x)‖² for all x.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No convexity equivalence, error bound in distance, or convergence rate is asserted by this terminology question.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Read the PL inequality, objective gap and parameter normalization; do not derive an iteration bound.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The local iteration theorem uses a more general algebraic PL hypothesis and a totalized gradient. This introductory differentiable-function QA is not an exact aligned Lean task.
mathematical_cores.question: What is the objective gap, what does the PL inequality compare, and is convexity part of this definition? Identify the roles of α and the gradient. Do not infer a gradient-descent rate without a step rule and a descent estimate.

rubric.criterion: Identifies f(x)−f* and explains its nonnegativity.
States the gap versus squared-gradient comparison with the correct factor 2α.
Does not include convexity or a distance conclusion in the definition.
Separates the condition from an algorithmic convergence theorem.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original definition-reading companion to the existing local PL iteration result.
steps: The objective gap is f(x)−f*, which is nonnegative by global minimality. The parameter α is a positive PL modulus in the stated factor-two convention.
The inequality \[2\alpha(f(x)-f_*)\le\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\] compares an objective-value gap with squared gradient norm. It is not a bound on distance to z.
Convexity is not one of the stated PL hypotheses. Do not insert a convexity or strong-convexity premise just because these conditions often appear in nearby optimization theorems.
An algorithmic rate additionally needs an actual update, a step restriction and a suitable decrease estimate. This question is about the condition itself, not that convergence proof.
mathematical_cores.title: Reading a PL inequality before using an algorithm

assumptions: S is the unit sphere in ℝᵈ with d≥2, equipped with its induced Euclidean metric. A real-valued function f is smooth on a neighborhood of S. Let w∈S.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No general manifold gradient API, retraction theorem, curvature comparison or optimization rate is claimed.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Identify the tangent-vector domain and metric-dependent gradient characterization before carrying out a projection proof.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The local theorem verifies this characterization for a specific feature potential. It is not a complete formalization of this general introductory definition QA.
mathematical_cores.question: Identify the tangent space at w and the defining directional-derivative identity for the gradient of f restricted to S. In what sense does this differ from the ambient Euclidean gradient? Do not prove an optimization convergence theorem.

rubric.criterion: States the tangent space as the orthogonal complement of the unit normal w.
Places G in the tangent space and quantifies the derivative identity over tangent directions.
Distinguishes ambient directions from induced-metric tangent directions.
Keeps the sphere/metric setting explicit without claiming arbitrary-manifold or convergence results.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original induced-sphere-metric definition exercise, supported by the existing feature-gradient instance.
steps: The tangent space is \[T_wS=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:\langle w,v\rangle=0\}.\] Its vectors are ambient vectors subject to an orthogonality condition.
The sphere gradient is the tangent vector G satisfying ⟨G,v⟩=Df(w)[v] for every v∈T_wS, using the induced inner product.

The ambient gradient represents derivatives in all ambient directions; it need not itself be tangent. Its orthogonal projection onto T_wS represents the same derivative on the allowed tangent directions.
This is the induced-metric sphere setting. Other manifolds and metrics need their own tangent spaces and gradient characterizations, not an automatic reuse of an ambient formula.
mathematical_cores.title: Which space contains the sphere gradient?

assumptions: μ,ν are Borel probability measures on ℝᵈ. A candidate joint measure γ is defined on ℝᵈ×ℝᵈ. No transport cost function or independence assumption is imposed on a general coupling.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No existence of an optimal plan, uniqueness, or Wasserstein metric theorem is asserted.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Identify the two marginal constraints and distinguish a feasible coupling from an optimal one.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The local coupling definition and product-coupling theorem support the stated concepts. No equivalent Lean task for the entire explanation is admitted.
mathematical_cores.question: State the two marginal identities that make γ a coupling of μ and ν. Is independence part of the definition? Identify a canonical feasible coupling and explain why feasibility alone does not mean optimality.

rubric.criterion: States both marginal identities with the correct coordinate order.
Does not assume independence for every coupling.
Identifies the product measure as a feasible probability coupling.
Distinguishes feasibility from cost optimality.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original coupling-definition exercise over the local transport foundation.
steps: For every Borel A,B, the marginal constraints are \[\gamma(A\times\mathbb R^d)=\mu(A),\qquad\gamma(\mathbb R^d\times B)=\nu(B).\] Equivalently the coordinate pushforwards are μ and ν.
A coupling specifies a joint law with these marginals; it need not be independent. Correlation is allowed as long as the marginal constraints remain satisfied.
The independent product is a canonical feasible coupling: \[(\mu\otimes\nu)(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B).\] Its marginals use the total masses equal to one.
Optimality requires a specified cost and a comparison of its integral over feasible plans. No optimality follows from the marginal identities alone.
mathematical_cores.title: What information does a coupling contain?

assumptions: The state space is a Boolean cube with m≥1 sites and target probability μ. For each site i, Kᵢ is the fixed coordinate heat-bath kernel, including its specified version on target-null fibers.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No efficient conditional-sampling implementation, ergodicity, mixing time or sweep complexity is asserted.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Read the time unit and update law of random scan without deriving balance, mixing or computational cost.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The source defines the actual uniform random-site mixture, with m=n+1. The complete terminology and time-convention QA is not an aligned proof-completion task.
mathematical_cores.question: Describe one uniform random-scan step and its mixture kernel. How does that time unit differ from a sweep of all sites? Does the mixture-law description itself specify a mixing time or an oracle-query cost?

rubric.criterion: Describes one uniformly chosen coordinate update with other coordinates retained.
States the 1/m mixture kernel and allows an unchanged state.
Distinguishes a single step from a scheduled sweep.
Does not infer a mixing or query-cost bound from the law definition.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original introductory reading of the local noncomputable random-scan transition law.
steps: One step first chooses one site I uniformly among the m sites, then draws the new state with kernel K_I, retaining the other coordinates.
The transition law is the state-independent mixture \[K(x,A)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}K_i(x,A).\] A coordinate resampling may return its previous value, so an update need not change the state.
A sweep applies coordinate updates across all sites according to a specified schedule; it is not this single random-site kernel step. Comparing bounds requires the same time convention.

A noncomputable transition-law definition alone supplies neither an implemented conditional sampler, its query cost, nor a mixing-time estimate. Those guarantees require additional algorithmic and analytic results.
mathematical_cores.title: One random-site step is not one sweep

assumptions: P is a finite row-stochastic transition matrix: P(x,y)≥0 and Σ_y P(x,y)=1. π and ρ are probability row vectors. Use total variation when discussing convergence.
mathematical_cores.boundary: No irreducibility, aperiodicity, mixing-rate theorem or general-state-space ergodic theorem is proved.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Distinguish three standard finite-chain definitions and keep the Markov normalization explicit.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The local atomic-balance result supports the reversibility notion. The finite-matrix definition comparison and identity-kernel example have no admitted aligned Lean view here.
mathematical_cores.question: Write the identities defining invariance and detailed balance for π. State what convergence from ρ means in this setting. Which identity controls one step started exactly in π, and why is that not the definition of convergence from an arbitrary start?

rubric.criterion: States πP=π with the correct one-step meaning.
States pairwise detailed balance and retains row-stochastic normalization.
Defines convergence from ρ as a limit of its time-t output laws in the given metric.
Does not substitute invariance or reversibility for an arbitrary-start convergence statement.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original finite-chain terminology exercise with an elementary identity-matrix illustration.
steps: Invariance is πP=π, or Σ_x π(x)P(x,y)=π(y) for each y. Starting exactly in π therefore gives the same law after one step.
Detailed balance is π(x)P(x,y)=π(y)P(y,x) for every x,y. Summing over x and using the row sum of P at y yields invariance; the stochastic normalization is part of that deduction.
Convergence from ρ is \[\operatorname{TV}(\rho P^t,\pi)\longrightarrow0\quad(t\to\infty).\] It concerns an entire sequence of laws from the specified start, not just the identity πP=π.
For the identity matrix P, every π is invariant and reversible, but ρP^t=ρ for all t. If ρ≠π, convergence to π fails. Thus one-step invariance is not a definition of general-start convergence.
mathematical_cores.title: Invariant, reversible and convergent are different claims
